sailor.text: Back to Aberdeen? We sail with the tide and the weather. The weather is currently 'interesting'. Hold on to your hat and your lunch.

cathedral_guide.text: St Magnus was begun in 1137, and it took three hundred years to finish. The builders ran out of money, then stone, then patience. The red and yellow sandstone makes stripes in the arches, like a very solemn sweet shop.
The cathedral has never had a bishop's palace next door that lasted. The ruin by the door is the Bishop's Palace, and it's a good place to practise your dramatic sigh.

ba_player.text: I've played the Ba' for twenty years. Uppie, born south of the cathedral. Doonie, born north. A baby born in the town is an Uppie or Doonie from its first day. My sister's a Doonie, which is basically a different nationality.
The ball's made of leather, stuffed with cork, and weighs a kilo and a bit. It's not thrown, it's pushed along by a hundred people at once. A scrum with a street in it.

stone_scholar.text: The Ring of Brodgar's about as old as Stonehenge. The Neolithic people of Orkney built stone houses, a great tomb at Maeshowe, and the stone circle, and they lined them up with the sun. They were serious about their calendars.
I'm counting the stones. I get 27, every time. A sheep behind me gets a different number. She's just very confident.

orkney_fisher.text: On a clear winter night the northern lights dance over the water. We call them the Merry Dancers. You'll be in the kitchen, and your gran will say 'quick, they're out'.
Orkney's mostly flat, with the sea in every direction. It's windy. The kind of wind that has opinions about your hat, and a plan.

then.text: A standing stone. Of course. We've been saying it for four and a half thousand years, and nobody's thought of a better answer.
Mind the sheep. They're not stones, but they've the same sort of patience.

else.text: Welcome to the Ring of Brodgar. Twenty-seven stones still stand of sixty, in a circle a hundred and four metres wide. Nobody wrote down why they built it. Not a single minute.

The schoolchildren ask me riddles all day, so here's one back for the grown-ups. I was raised to stand in a ring. I've outlived everyone who raised me. Wind and rain and councils have all had a go, and I'm still here, quite upright.

then.text: Ha! You're quick. There's a prize in the van: a couple of bottles of tonic, the fizzy sort. Don't ask what's in it.

else.text: Ah, no. Nearly. Have another think, and mind that the answer is, strictly, a good deal older than any ferry captain.

then.text: The Ring is still. A few sheep gaze at you, politely, as if you were a standing stone that had decided to wander.
Somebody has left a kettle on a flat rock. It is, somehow, still warm.
The wind drops. All at once, the way it never does in Orkney. The stones of the Ring stand against a sky so full of stars it looks overbooked.
A figure in an oilskin sits on a fallen stone, a lantern at their feet. They don't seem surprised. They seem pleased, like a host.
Good evening. You've walked a long way. Everyone who comes at night has. It's the only time the Ring talks.
Four and a half thousand years it's been stood here. It's heard every argument, every proposal and every bad song. It has opinions on all of them.
It doesn't tell most folk. But it's watched you. The Stones you carry, the legends you've been kind to. It likes kind.
A low hum rises from the ground, the same hum Professor Garside once complained about, only gentler. It sounds like the world clearing its throat.
Here. Take this. It fell off the Ring a long time ago and has been waiting for someone to ask for it.
Keep it in your pocket. It won't do anything. That's the whole point of it. Mind, now. Somebody wants to say hello.
Well. That's that. The Ring's said its piece. Go home, and mind the sheep on the way.

else.text: A shepherd's coat has been left over a stone. A lantern sits beside it, unlit. Nobody's about.
The Ring feels like a held breath. Whatever it's holding, it won't let go in daylight. Perhaps after dark.
Just a stone, standing in a field of Orkney, with the wind going round it. Nothing more to see here. Yet.
